COMMENTS OF BRIGHTNIGHT POWER MARKETING, LLC 
 
BrightNight Power Marketing, LLC (“BrightNight”)1 submits these Comments in 
response to the Commission’s Order Instituting Proceeding Under Section 206 of the Federal 
Power Act (“FPA”) and Consolidating with Other Proceedings2 and the answers filed by PJM 
Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) and individual and groups of PJM Transmission Owners (“PJM 
TOs”).3  BrightNight appreciates the opportunity to share its on-the-ground perspective on co-
 
1  
BrightNight is filing these comments pursuant to Rule 211 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the 
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“Commission”), 18 C.F.R. § 385.211, having intervened in 
Docket No. EL25-49-000 on March 12, 2025. 
2  
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al., 190 FERC ¶ 61,115 (2025) (“Show Cause Order”).  In the Show Cause 
Order, the Commission directed PJM and the PJM Transmissions to either explain why the existing PJM 
governing documents are just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential without 
provisions specifically addressing co-located load arrangements or explain what changes would remedy the 
Commission’s concerns. Id. at P 87. 
3  
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al., Docket No. EL25-49-000, Answer of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
(Mar. 24, 2025) (“PJM Answer”); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al., Docket No. EL25-49-000, Answer 
of the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners (Mar. 24, 2025) (“Indicated PJM Transmission Owners 
Answer”); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al., Docket No. EL25-49-000, Response of Public Service

3 
 
location issues.  BrightNight works with all types of customers around the United States to 
design, develop, and operate safe, reliable, large-scale, power projects.  BrightNight is an active 
developer of renewable and other types of generation projects and is in discussions with data 
centers interested in co-locating with hybrid renewable generation.  There is significant potential 
in the co-location model to (i) meet the ever-increasing energy needs of data centers while (ii) 
supporting reliability and reducing congestion on the grid and (iii) ensuring that data center load 
pays its fair share of costs.  To successfully achieve these interrelated goals, the industry must 
have regulatory certainty without foreclosing flexible commercial approaches.  Because PJM’s 
current open access transmission tariff is not sufficiently clear about the rules that apply to co-
located load arrangements, BrightNight supports the Commission establishing pro forma rules, 
not only for PJM but rules that could apply more broadly, for evaluating and serving co-located 
load and generation that provide certainty for participants but include flexibility so as to not 
unnecessarily stifle innovative arrangements.  Any rates or charges applicable to co-located load 
must be just and reasonable by requiring co-located load to pay only for the grid services that it 
needs and benefits from, and ensures that co-located load does not directly or indirectly cross-
subsidize other customers.  Additionally, BrightNight supports an expedited or fast-tracked study 
process for co-located load and generation. 
I. 
BACKGROUND 
 
As technology has advanced to seamlessly connect people and systems across industries, 
the need for large, external facilities that store and process large amounts of digital data, e.g., 
 
Electric and Gas Company (“PSEG”) (Mar. 24, 2025) (“PSEG Answer”); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et 
al., Docket No. EL25-49-000, Answer of the Dayton Power and Light Company D/B/A AES Ohio (Mar. 
24, 2025); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al., Docket No. EL25-49-000, Answer of Allegheny Electric 
Cooperative, Inc. (Mar. 24, 2025); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al., Docket No. EL25-49-000, Answer 
of NextEra Energy Transmission MidAtlantic, Inc. (Mar. 24, 2025); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al., 
Docket No. EL25-49-000, Answer of Silver Run Electric, LLC (Mar. 24, 2025).

4 
 
data centers, has increased.  Data centers require a significant amount of electricity to operate 
servers and cooling systems.  The dramatic increase in data center demand is expected to result 
in significant load growth on an electric system that had been forecasting flat load growth.  The 
Department of Energy’s 2024 Report on U.S. Data Center Energy Use estimates that data center 
load growth has tripled over the past decade and will double or triple again by 2028.4  In 
response to long wait periods to interconnect and obtain service from the grid, data center 
developers are exploring solutions that include co-locating with generation but are running into 
barriers. 
 
In response to challenges associated with the co-located load model, the Commission 
convened a technical conference on November 1, 2024, to examine the issues in Docket NO. 
AD24-11-000 (“Co-location Technical Conference”).5  Later that same month, Constellation 
Energy Generation, LLC (“Constellation”) filed a complaint under Section 206 of the FPA, 
arguing that PJM’s Tariff is unjust and unreasonable and unduly discriminatory because it does 
not contain rules or guidance for generators to follow when interconnecting to provide service to 
a fully isolated co-located load.6  Constellation explained that, while nothing in the PJM Tariff 
prohibits fully isolated co-located load arrangements, utilities have relied upon ambiguities in the 
rules to thwart competition by delaying or significantly increasing the costs of such 
 
4  
DOE Press Release, DOE Releases New Report Evaluating Increase in Electricity Demand from Data 
Centers (Dec. 20, 2024), available at https://www.energy.gov/articles/doe-releases-new-report-evaluating-
increase-electricity-demand-data-centers. 
5  
Large Loads Co-Located at Generating Facilities, Docket No. AD24-11-000, Notice of Commissioner-Led 
Technical Conference (Aug. 2, 2024).  The Commission requested that interested parties file post-technical 
conference comments, but took no further action in the docket until the Show Cause Order. 
6  
Constellation Energy Generation, LLC v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. EL25-20-000, 
Complaint Requesting Fast Track Processing of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC at 1 (Nov. 22, 
2024) (“Constellation Complaint”).

5 
 
arrangements.7  Constellation asked the Commission to require PJM to incorporate into its Tariff 
sections from PJM’s Guidance on Co-located Load.8 
 
On February 20, 2025, the Commission issued the Show Cause Order opening a new 
docket, Docket No. EL24-49-000, and consolidated the new docket with the Constellation 
Complaint docket, Docket No. EL25-20-000, and the technical conference docket exploring co-
located large loads and generators, Docket No. AD24-11-000.  Based on the Constellation 
Complaint and Co-location Technical Conference, the Commission found that PJM’s Tariff 
appears to be unjust, unreasonable, unduly discriminatory or preferential, and directed PJM and 
PJM Transmission Owners to either:  
(1) show cause as to why the [PJM Tariff], the Amended and 
Restated Operating Agreement of PJM, and Reliability Assurance 
Agreement Among Load Serving Entities in the PJM Region . . . 
remains just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or 
preferential without provisions addressing with sufficient clarity or 
consistency the rates, terms, and conditions of service that apply to 
co-location arrangements; or (2) explain what changes to the Tariff 
would remedy the identified concerns if the Commission were to 
determine that the Tariff has in fact become unjust and 
unreasonable or unduly discriminatory or preferential and, 
therefore, proceeds to establish a replacement Tariff.9 
PJM and PJM Transmission Owners filed answers and responses.  PJM took the position 
that the PJM Tariff is just and reasonable, although it conceded that there is room for 
improvements and clarifications.10  It asked the Commission to provide guidance so that it can 
move forward.11  PJM included in its answer eight potential co-location arrangements and 
 
7

8  
Id. at 2.

10

summarized what it sees as each arrangement’s key attributes, impacts on the grid, necessary 
studies, rates, operational considerations, and service options.12  PJM expressed a preference for 
certain options and less of a preference for other options.13    Indicated PJM Transmission 
Owners urged the Commission to find that the existing PJM Tariff is just and reasonable and 
declare that all co-located loads should be treated as load in front of the meter and designated as 
Network Load.14  PSEG, a transmission owner who filed separately from other transmission 
owners, framed the question before the Commission as defining what benefits a particular co-
located load and generation configuration receives from the grid and setting charges and rates 
accordingly.15 
II. 
COMMENTS 
A. 
Develop Pro Forma Co-location Interconnection Procedures and Agreements 
The comments across the three dockets show that Commission guidance is needed, and it 
is needed now.  Data center developers, generation developers, and system planners cannot make 
long-term decisions without understanding what co-location arrangements the Commission will 
accept.  Ideally, Commission guidance would come in the form of pro forma procedures and 
agreements governing co-location arrangements.  Standardizing procedures and agreements 
would give developers and planners certainty, reduce opportunities for undue discrimination or 
 
12  
PJM Answer at Exhibit A. 
13  
Id. 
14  
Indicated PJM Transmission Owners Answers at 2. 
15  
PSEG Answer at 1-2.

7 
 
preference, reduce disputes, and, hopefully, expedite the development of data centers and needed 
generation.16  
While standardization is beneficial, it is equally important that the Commission build into 
any pro forma procedures and agreements flexibility to allow for different co-location 
configurations and arrangements.  Not all large loads are the same, so not all co-location 
configurations will be the same either.17  This could be accomplished by allowing different paths 
that lead to different studies and services for different types of co-location configurations.  The 
type of co-location arrangement can then lead to different charges.18  A pro forma process and 
agreements should allow for at least the following three configurations: (i) load and generation 
are fully islanded from the electric grid, with no service from the grid; (ii) flexible loads or 
demand response loads; and (iii) loads that will require backup grid service, such as a behind the 
meter arrangement, with associated studies and costs for each.  Furthermore, the resulting 
services and charges applicable to each of these configurations should impose charges on load 
and generation based only on the transmission services used and benefits received from the grid.  
 
16  
The benefits of standardized procedures and arrangements for co-located load and generation are similar to 
those the Commission found for generator interconnection.  See, e.g., Order No. 2003 at PP 8-12. See 
Standardization of Generator Interconnection Agreements & Procs., Order No. 2003,104 FERC ¶ 61,103 
at PP 8-12 (2003), order on reh’g, Order No. 2003-A, 106 FERC ¶ 61,220, order on reh’g, Order No. 
2003-B, 109 FERC ¶ 61,287 (2004), order on reh’g, Order No. 2003-C, 111 FERC ¶ 61,401 (2005), aff’d 
sub nom. Nat’l Ass’n of Regul. Util. Comm’rs v. FERC, 475 F.3d 1277 (D.C. Cir. 2007). 
17  
See Large Loads Co-located at Generating Facilities, Docket No. AD24-11-000, Post-Workshop Comments 
of the Solar Energy Industries Association at 4 (Dec. 9, 2024) (“SEIA Post-Technical Conference 
Comments”), citing Kormos Pre-filed Presentation, The Co-Located Load Solution at 2.  PJM identified 
eight potential co-location configurations that have different needs and impacts on the grid.  PJM Answer at 
Exhibit A. 
18  
Data center developers have agreed that they should pay for the benefits they receive from the grid.  See 
Large Loads Co-located at Generating Facilities, Docket No. AD24-11-000, Post-Workshop Comments of 
the Data Center Coalition at 5 (Dec. 9, 2024) (“Consistent with established and sound utility ratemaking 
principles, DCC’s co-location principles support all load paying their fair share of costs for benefits and 
services received from the grid, including transmission, energy, and ancillary services costs.” (citation 
omitted)); Large Loads Co-located at Generating Facilities, Docket No. AD24-11-000, Post-Workshop 
Comments of Google LLC at 5 (Dec. 9, 2024) (At Google, we are not seeking to avoid paying our fair 
share of these costs . . ..”).

8 
 
In this respect, BrightNight generally supports the PSEG approach and strongly disagrees with 
the ‘one-size fits all configurations’ approach put forward by indicated PJM Transmission 
Owners.  Co-located load should be charged just and reasonable rates and not forced to subsidize 
other customers.    
BrightNight also supports the Co-Location Interconnection Service Agreement concept 
proposed by the Solar Energy Industries Association (“SEIA”) in its post-technical conference 
comments in Docket No. AD24-11-000.19  SEIA urged the Commission to adopt a pro forma but 
flexible approach for co-location arrangements, particular fully islanded load and generation; 
flexible loads or demand responsive load; and loads that require back-up gride service.20  SEIA 
suggested that the Commission define the problem and impact of various types of co-location 
arrangements and develop a pro forma agreement considering different arrangements.21  As 
stated, “The pro forma agreement would provide flexibility in its terms to accommodate various 
types of co-location arrangements, including load receiving firm transmission service or load that 
does not receive full transmission service.  Included in the pro forma agreement would be 
provisions for System Protection Facilities in place to prevent the unexpected withdrawal of 
power from the grid, and penalties for failure of these protection facilities.”22  The Commission 
can use the record created in this proceeding to establish a pro forma agreement for co-locating 
loads and generation in the PJM region that set the baseline for other regions and transmission 
providers to use. 
 
19  
SEIA Post-Technical Conference Comments at 5-6. 
20  
Id. at 4. 
21  
Id. at 3-5. 
22  
Id. at 5-6.

9 
 
B. 
Rules Should Incentivize Co-Located Load to Bring Its Own Generation 
In its answer, PJM recognized that large load bringing its own generation has benefits.23  
While large load should not be required to bring its own generation, BrightNight agrees that 
there are significant benefits when large load brings new generation with it, particularly if that 
generation is co-located with the large load.  Large load bringing new generation promotes 
resource adequacy and avoids new constraints or congestion on the transmission system.   
In its answer, PJM discusses ways to incentivize large loads to bring their own 
generation, including expedited interconnection studies.24  SEIA outlined a process that 
incentivizes load to bring its own generation in its Post-Technical Conference Comments.25  An 
expedited or fast-tracked interconnection process appears to be appropriate.  PJM should be 
required to net the large load and generation, resulting in faster study time and less impact on the 
transmission system and load forecast.  It could be handled similarly to the surplus 
interconnection process, where the load and generation configuration can be screened for 
potential material impacts to the native transmission system or adjoining systems.  If there are 
material impacts that cannot be resolved among the affected systems, then the load and 
generation will be shifted to the typical interconnection and transmission service request 
processes.  BrightNight encourages the Commission, PJM, and other stakeholders to incorporate 
in the pro forma co-location procedures incentives for large loads to bring co-located generation. 
 
23  
PJM Answer at 16-18, Exhibit A. 
24  
Id. at 17. 
25  
SEIA Post-Technical Conference Comments at 6-7.

10 
 
III. 
CONCLUSION 
BrightNight respectfully requests that the Commission consider these comments as it 
contemplates how to move forward on co-location issues in PJM. 
April 23, 2025
